routes.description: Establish consciousness as the sole fundamental ontology and explain objective order, individual perspectives, causality, and nonspatiotemporal structure as configurations of universal subjectivity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if a consciousness-only ontology avoids emergence while accounting for empirical regularity, external reality, differentiated subjects, causal efficacy, and structured relations without fundamental spacetime.

motionBridge.description: Show that consciousness is a more parsimonious and explanatorily complete ontological foundation than non-conscious matter or neutral primitives.

centralBridges.description: Explain how an observer-independent and scientifically ordered world can consist of external mental states represented through perception.
Explain individual selves and experiences as differentiated modes or excitations of one universal subjectivity.
Ground causal regularity in intrinsic properties and interactions within a single mental ontology.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect physics, neuroscience, altered experience, and consciousness theory to predictions or implications consistent with idealism.
Account for fundamental structure through semantic or cognitive relations that do not require spatial or temporal extension.

routes.description: Deny that failures of materialist emergence establish idealism by developing a neutral representational alternative and testing whether idealism explains structure, causality, and subjecthood.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if neutral representational processes avoid the hard problem while consciousness-first language fails to add necessary explanatory content concerning ordered structure, causal agents, or experience.

motionBridge.description: Show that avoiding matter-to-consciousness emergence does not require treating consciousness as the ontological foundation of reality.

centralBridges.description: Locate phenomenal character in representations without positing either separately existing physical objects or universal consciousness as substance.
Require an account of how representations, organism boundaries, and predictable order arise rather than merely labeling their inaccessible substrate mental.
Determine where causal efficacy resides when the ordinary personal self is constructed, unstable, or absent.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish correlations or mappings involving integrated information from an explanation of why subjective experience exists.
Test whether theories framed through brains, fields, vibrations, or processes can accommodate experience without ordinary space and time.

sections.title: Ontological foundation and empirical warrant
sections.rationale: The motion turns first on whether consciousness is the most economical fundamental given and whether available empirical considerations distinguish that proposal from a neutral alternative.

sections.title: External reality and explanatory structure
sections.rationale: A consciousness-first ontology must preserve an observer-independent ordered world and specify how perception, organisms, and regularities arise within its single category.

sections.title: Representation, self-models, and experience
sections.rationale: The distribution of phenomenal character across representations and the status of the personal self determine whether neutral representation suffices or still presupposes consciousness.

sections.title: Integrated information and explanatory scope
sections.rationale: Integrated information bears on the persistence and causal role of experience, but its relevance depends on whether it supplies operational prediction, metaphysical explanation, or limited ontological implications.

sections.title: Subjecthood and the source of causality
sections.rationale: The ontology must identify the bearer and source of causal efficacy when personal selves are modeled as constructed and dream contents may arise without an experienced agent.

sections.title: Structure without fundamental spacetime
sections.rationale: The account of fundamental reality must preserve differentiation and meaningful structure even when ordinary spatial and temporal organization is absent or nonfundamental.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Consciousness is the sole pre-theoretical given and therefore the most parsimonious foundation for reality, whereas emergence from non-conscious physical quantities supplies no intelligible explanation of experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly addresses Bernardo, and the uninterrupted first-person answer consistently presents Kastrup's stated idealist position.

response.rationale: Constructive opening directly supplies the debate-wide parsimony case for a consciousness-only foundation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states both its starting point and reductionist inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The thesis and comparison are recoverable, although “pre-theoretical given” and the reach of parsimony need a bounded qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The stated preference for reduction supplies a plausible comparative case, but does not by itself establish ontological exclusivity.

charity.alternative: A neutral primitive could be equally parsimonious while consciousness is only epistemically immediate.
charity.decisiveQualification: Epistemic givenness does not alone establish ontological fundamentality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is intelligible but leaves a material bridge from epistemic priority and parsimony to ontological priority.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The hard-problem consideration supports the critique, while the exclusivity and comparative-parsimony warrants remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This directly advances the motion bridge by arguing for consciousness as the simplest sole foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly attacks emergence but only indirectly addresses the strongest neutral-primitive alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly invokes reduction to one pre-theoretical given, identifies that given as consciousness, and contrasts this with unexplained emergence.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Quantum measurement results, selected neuroscientific theories, and richer experience during reduced brain metabolism provide empirical considerations consistent with idealism.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage directly continues Bernardo's answer after the moderator requests evidence, with no indicated change of speaker until Susan is addressed.

response.rationale: Constructive empirical support connects several reported scientific considerations to consistency with idealism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves it offers relevant examples, though their evidential independence and implications are compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limited consistency claim is clear, but the referenced scientific theories and causal principle are insufficiently specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker expressly describes the implications as few and consistent with idealism rather than uniquely confirming it.

charity.alternative: The cited findings may be equally consistent with physicalist or neutral accounts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Consistency evidence does not discriminate among compatible ontologies.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference to compatibility is coherent and appropriately limited, with only the empirical-to-ontology bridge compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific categories of evidence are named, but representative results, rival comparison, and verification of the metabolic inference are limited.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially supports the subsidiary empirical-fit bridge without directly completing the motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The modest wording respects the live rival explanations, although the move does not compare them in detail.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly claims limited implications consistent with idealism and cites richer nonordinary experience alongside reduced brain metabolic activity.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Although matter-to-consciousness emergence creates a genuine hard problem, analytic idealism does not yet explain the world's ordered structure or justify its dissociation model, so neutral monism remains preferable.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly hands the discussion to Susan, and the ensuing first-person critique addresses Bernardo by name throughout the turn.

components.text: Whether avoiding unexplained emergence establishes consciousness as the uniquely preferable foundation.
Whether cited empirical compatibility discriminates idealism from a neutral alternative.

response.rationale: The reply concedes the emergence problem but denies that idealism has supplied the ordered-world and dissociation explanations needed for preference; it does not substantively assess the earlier empirical examples.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer contacting the decisive exclusivity inference while leaving the empirical-consistency component largely unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The concession, explanatory objection, and preference for neutral monism are distinguishable and clearly scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The position is presented as a preferred developing alternative, not as a demonstrated or certain ontology.

charity.alternative: Idealism may claim parsimony without yet providing a complete mechanistic derivation of worldly order.
charity.decisiveQualification: Incomplete derivation weakens explanatory completeness but does not erase the parsimony argument.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The underdetermination inference is coherent: a defect in emergence does not entail idealism when a neutral alternative remains live.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The explanatory demands are well identified, but neutral monism is asserted more than independently developed in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the con motion bridge by denying that anti-emergence considerations require idealism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants the hard problem and takes idealism seriously, though it somewhat compresses the distinction between ontology and mechanism.

moves.evidenceBasis: The passage concedes a real matter-to-consciousness problem while challenging idealism's explanation of structure and dissociation and retaining neutral monism.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Analytic idealism preserves a mind-independent external world by treating it as external mental states whose physical appearance is a perceptual representation rather than the represented reality itself.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan invites Bernardo to clarify his view, after which a sustained first-person explanation explicitly distinguishes Bernardo's internal states from the external world.

components.text: How idealism can preserve an observer-independent ordered external world rather than merely private qualities.
How the proposed dissociation model itself is justified.

response.rationale: The answer directly distinguishes perceived qualities from external mental states and thereby contacts the external-world demand, while leaving the separate dissociation warrant unresolved.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive external-world component is contacted clearly, but the broader explanatory objection receives only a partial answer.

precisionFindings.rationale: Internal perceptual qualities, external mental states, and mediated perception are consistently distinguished throughout the move.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conceptual model is coherently stated, but its confident presentation exceeds the support offered for identifying the external substrate as mental.

charity.alternative: The objection asks for generative structure, not merely permission for an external world.
charity.decisiveQualification: Preserving externality does not yet explain its detailed order or dissociation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The representation-versus-represented distinction coherently permits mind independence inside idealism, with one implicit identity premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument supplies a clear conceptual model but little independent warrant that external causes are specifically mental states.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the central objective-world bridge by preserving externality and mediated perception.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move answers a substantial version of the objection but does not fully engage its strongest explanatory-content form.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes internal colors and flavors from external mental states known through sense organs and explicitly affirms an external world.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Calling an inaccessible representational substrate mental neither explains its structure nor identifies how representations are constructed, and thus appears to add no explanatory content.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn follows Kastrup's extended clarification and directly challenges it in Susan's characteristic first-person representationalist framing.

components.text: Whether describing the inaccessible represented reality as mental adds an explanation of its structure.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges the inference from a representational external world to a specifically mental substrate and asks how representations and predictive organization arise.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts the decisive explanatory-content gap in the preceding external-mental-state proposal.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection clearly distinguishes adopting a mental label from explaining representation construction and predictive structure.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker frames this as a demand and an apparent explanatory deficit rather than a conclusive refutation.

charity.alternative: A metaphysical identity claim need not function as a detailed cognitive mechanism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even so, a route claiming explanatory completeness must connect that identity to organized representation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference that relabeling an unknown substrate does not by itself explain its organization is explicit and well bounded.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The representational and predictive-processing examples concretize the demand, though no detailed rival model is defended here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move squarely advances the central con explanatory-content bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection preserves the possible metaphysical role while pressing the legitimate missing explanatory bridge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks why predictive brains have their organization if all is mental and presses for the origin and substrate of representations.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: A single mental ontology removes the unnecessary category that creates the hard problem, while dissociation, mental causation, natural selection, and intrinsic dispositions can account for organisms and predictable physical order.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage begins as a direct answer to Susan's objection and continues as one sustained exposition of Kastrup's analytic-idealist framework.

components.text: How idealism explains representation, organism boundaries, causal interaction, and predictable order.
Why consciousness-first ontology is preferable to neutral monism.

response.rationale: The reply invokes sensory evolution, dissociation, mental-to-mental causation, and intrinsic dispositions while arguing that one ontology removes the hard-problem category split.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive demand with several mechanisms, but their derivation and the dissociation bridge remain materially compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The single-ontology thesis is recoverable, though “trivial” mental causation and intrinsic dispositions conceal substantive explanatory commitments.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The category-economy argument is supported, but describing mental-to-mental causation as unproblematic overstates what the supplied account establishes.

charity.alternative: The objection seeks an explanation of organization, not merely removal of an ontological category.
charity.decisiveQualification: Evolution and dissociation must themselves be grounded within the proposed mental ontology.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The unified-ontology inference is coherent, while the transitions from impingement to evolved organs and predictable order leave material bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move names mechanisms but largely asserts their availability, without detailed evidence or comparison with neutral alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the central mental-causation and objective-order requirements, with causality its strongest exact contact.

representationalCharity.rationale: The answer recognizes and attempts the generative demand, but treats several contested mental mechanisms as readily available.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes external mental states causally impinging on internal states, evolution amplifying that relation through sense organs, and a single mental category.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Neutral monism can avoid the hard problem by locating phenomenal character in a system's self-representation rather than in a separately existing physical object such as a bat.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly identifies herself as a neutral monist and develops her own alternative before requesting Bernardo's response.

components.text: Whether eliminating a physical category requires making universal consciousness the remaining substance.
Whether phenomenal character belongs to represented objects or to representations.

response.rationale: The reply proposes locating phenomenal character in self-representation rather than a separately existing represented object, thereby offering a neutral route around emergence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the ontology choice, though the positive neutral account remains exploratory and underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The represented-object distinction is clear, but “representation” and its neutral substrate are not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker expressly presents the view as something being explored rather than as an established conclusion.

charity.alternative: Idealism can also locate experience in representations while treating their substrate as mental.
charity.decisiveQualification: Representational relocation alone does not decide between neutral monism and idealism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Moving phenomenal character from an independent object to a representation is coherent, but the neutral-substrate bridge remains implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The proposal is conceptually motivated but receives little specific evidence or explanation of how representation acquires phenomenal character.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central neutral-representation bridge and the con route's principal alternative.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly targets a shared problem but only partially differentiates the neutral proposal from its idealist rival.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt denies that phenomenal character belongs to a separate physical bat and relocates it in the bat's representation while presenting neutral monism as exploratory.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Self-representations and illusory personal agents are compatible with idealism, but materialist illusionism generates a regress because every neural model still requires an account of why it is experienced.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo explicitly frames the response for the audience, refers to Susan's established view, and contrasts it with materialist illusionism and idealism.

components.text: Whether placing phenomenal character in representation avoids the need to explain why that representation is experienced.

response.rationale: The reply expressly identifies a regress: redescribing experience as a neural or self-model leaves the model's experienced character unexplained, while idealism already permits experienced illusion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly attacks the decisive inference and states the defeating consequence for a representation-only escape from the hard problem.

precisionFindings.rationale: Materialist illusionism is clearly distinguished from the compatibility of illusory self-models with idealism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The regress objection is forcefully stated but properly conditioned on a materialist model being offered as the full explanation.

charity.alternative: A neutral representationalist may treat phenomenal character as identical with representation, not as an added experience.
charity.decisiveQualification: That identity still needs clarification if it is to explain rather than stipulate phenomenal character.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regress diagnosis is explicit and coherent: a model description alone does not answer why modeling has phenomenal character.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument is primarily conceptual and strong within that scope, but does not compare all neutral representational identity options.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central neutral-representation bridge by restoring the phenomenal-explanation demand.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move captures the strongest explanatory demand, though its materialist framing does not exhaust every neutral identity theory.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes self-delusive models but argues that illusions are still experienced and that materialist model descriptions reproduce the explanatory demand.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Phenomenal character should extend beyond the unstable self-model to representations throughout a cognitive hierarchy, including simple and fleeting lower-level models.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker responds to Bernardo's conclusion, then develops a first-person proposal grounded in predictive hierarchies, meditation, and self-model dissolution.

response.rationale: Constructive proposal broadens phenomenal character from the narrative self-model to representations across the cognitive hierarchy.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves it supplies a relevant distributional proposal, but presents it mainly as a question for development.

precisionFindings.rationale: The hierarchy-wide proposal is recoverable, although “something it is like” and the boundary of qualifying models remain open.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker asks whether the proposal should extend to other models and labels it a possible representational panpsychism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Extending phenomenal status beyond an unstable self-model is internally coherent, but lacks a criterion for which representations qualify.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cognitive-hierarchy observation motivates the question, while the attribution of phenomenal character remains speculative.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally develops the con neutral-representation route by specifying a distributed locus of phenomenal character.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span develops an exploratory positive proposal rather than evaluating a sufficiently specified competing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts the small contribution to the phenomenal self-model with extensive other processing and asks whether all such models have phenomenal character.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Ego dissolution leaves experience intact, and integrated information theory supports the view that informational complexes excluded from the narrative self can retain their own subjective perspectives.
moves.attributionBasis: The response addresses Susan by name, contrasts her meditation experience with Bernardo's psychedelic experience, and then explicitly introduces his interpretation of IIT.

components.text: Whether experience can persist outside the narrative self-model and across other informational complexes.
Whether representations presuppose phenomenal subjectivity rather than explain it.

response.rationale: The reply affirms experience during ego dissolution and uses IIT exclusion to assign shed informational complexes their own subjective perspectives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly contacts distribution beyond the self-model, though the IIT-to-subjectivity warrant remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: Ego, maximal complex, and subjective perspective are identifiable, but their exact equivalence within IIT is not fully stabilized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Persistence of experience without ego is well framed, but assigning every excluded complex its own perspective exceeds the stated support.

charity.alternative: Distributed representations could have phenomenal character without being modes of universal consciousness.
charity.decisiveQualification: IIT's complex structure alone does not settle the ontology of phenomenal character.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The ego-dissolution inference is coherent, but the bridge from excluded informational complexes to separate subjective perspectives is material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Reported ego dissolution and IIT terminology provide some support, while the metaphysical conclusion remains largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally advances subject differentiation by locating experience in complexes beyond the narrative self.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move addresses distributed character but moves too quickly from IIT complexes to explicitly mental subjects.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies the ego with a maximal IIT complex and claims that informational material excluded from it retains a subjective point of view.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Integrated information theory's correlation between integrated information and degrees of consciousness does not explain why there is anything it is like to be a system.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker directly addresses Kastrup's superior familiarity with IIT and asks him to clarify its account of consciousness.

components.text: Whether IIT's integration measures explain why an informational complex has any subjective perspective.

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes a relationship between integration and reported consciousness from an explanation of why experience exists at all.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts the decisive IIT-to-subjectivity warrant, while acknowledging limited command of IIT's technical details.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes graded correlation from an explanation of phenomenal existence and explicitly limits its technical claim.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker openly acknowledges uncertainty and poses a targeted explanatory question rather than claiming IIT has been disproved.

charity.alternative: IIT may offer an identity claim rather than a conventional causal explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: An identity claim still requires defense of why integration and experience are the same property.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The correlation-versus-explanation distinction is explicit, consistent, and directly challenges the relevant inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The objection accurately targets the stated mapping, though it does not engage IIT's complete axiomatic identity argument.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It is at the top of the subsidiary IIT-gap tier because it states that bridge's exact explanatory demand.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection is narrowly framed and leaves room for a stronger metaphysical interpretation while preserving its decisive demand.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt acknowledges technical limitations but precisely asks why greater integrated information entails anything-it-is-like rather than merely tracking reports.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: At its operational level, integrated information theory maps measurable substrate states to reported experience and makes predictions without purporting to define consciousness metaphysically.
moves.attributionBasis: The response follows Blackmore's request for clarification and uses Kastrup's characteristic first-person framing of IIT's limited scientific role.

components.text: What IIT must establish if its role here is operational prediction rather than metaphysical explanation.

response.rationale: The reply justifies replacing the metaphysical demand with an operational one at IIT's first level, where measurable substrate states predict otherwise unavailable consciousness reports.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe explicitly limits IIT's task and answers the preserved issue of what evidential work the theory performs.

precisionFindings.rationale: Operational, scientific, philosophical, and metaphysical roles are clearly separated and the limitation to a first level is explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical language is proportionate to the expressly limited claim that this level is operational rather than metaphysical.

charity.alternative: The original objection remains relevant if IIT is later used to support claims about subjective existence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Operational success does not close the metaphysical explanatory gap.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The scope distinction is explicit and valid: an operational map can succeed without answering the metaphysical question.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The coma and report-inference example concretely supports operational usefulness, with detailed validation evidence outside this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly addresses the subsidiary IIT bridge by delimiting what the mapping establishes and what it does not.

representationalCharity.rationale: The answer accurately preserves the objection outside the limited operational role and does not pretend prediction explains experience.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites inference about consciousness where reports are unavailable and explicitly characterizes IIT as measurable operational prediction rather than metaphysics.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Although integrated information theory is compatible with materialism, its account of causal complexes and existence-for-itself gives it limited idealist implications.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted explanation continues Kastrup's answer and explicitly marks the conclusions as modest ontological implications of IIT.

components.text: Whether IIT's causal-complex language supports any ontological conclusion about existence for itself.

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes experienced contents from causally integrated complexes and claims limited idealist implications while expressly allowing materialist IIT.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the ontological question but only partially answers the why-experience demand and carefully limits the implication.

precisionFindings.rationale: The complex-versus-content distinction is recoverable, though “exists for itself” remains technically and philosophically compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker repeatedly conditions the idealist implication and expressly states that IIT can be pursued under materialism.

charity.alternative: Causal integration may be described wholly within materialism without phenomenal ontology.
charity.decisiveQualification: Compatibility with idealism is not independent evidence for idealism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional conclusion is coherent, but the inference from causal complex to existence-for-itself retains a substantive implicit bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: IIT's exclusion distinction supports the structural claim, while the idealist interpretation lacks independent comparative warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially supports empirical fit through IIT but does not directly complete a central ontological bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move explicitly concedes the strongest materialist interpretation and claims only limited conditional implications.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes an experienced green elephant from an integrated causal complex and explicitly qualifies IIT's idealist implications and materialist compatibility.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Assigning causal power to the dreaming subject remains unclear if the self is not what it appears to be and the imagined object lacks causal power.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker thanks Kastrup for his explanation, restates his green-elephant example, and challenges what his use of the first person denotes.

components.text: Which subject or complex bears causal power when the personal self is conceded to be constructed.
How a subjective perspective is individuated from the unstable ego model.

response.rationale: The reply directly presses the identity of the causal “I” after agreement that ordinary selves are not what they appear to be.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly isolates the decisive bearer-of-causation gap created by the preceding self and complex claims.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast among imagined object, causal speaker, and unstable self is clear and needs no further scope qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move is a precisely calibrated request for clarification rather than an unsupported assertion that no answer is possible.

charity.alternative: The causal subject could be a deeper experiential complex rather than the narrative self.
charity.decisiveQualification: The theory must specify that deeper bearer and its individuation conditions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The challenge follows directly from the conceded instability of self and the denial of autonomous causal power to dream content.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The objection relies on explicit commitments already made and identifies their unresolved conjunction without speculative factual premises.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly reaches the central con causal-subject bridge and states its decisive requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The question leaves the deeper-subject answer open while accurately identifying the remaining explanatory requirement.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks what “you” means in the claim that the speaker causes a dream elephant after both parties questioned the ordinary self's reality.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Experiences are excitations of a universal core subjectivity rather than separable contents, and individual selves are modes of that single underlying subjectivity.
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup explicitly separates IIT's answer from his own philosophical interpretation and develops the core-subjectivity account in a continuous response.

components.text: What subject remains when the personal self dissolves and can serve as the bearer of experience.

response.rationale: The answer identifies universal core subjectivity as the enduring bearer and treats individuals as patterned excitations or modes of it.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly answers the identity question at the ontological level, though causal individuation is not yet fully explained.

precisionFindings.rationale: Core subjectivity and excitations remain consistent, but the scope of “one thing that really exists” needs an implicit metaphysical qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Ego-dissolution reports support experience without a narrative ego, but not by themselves the certainty of one universal subject.

charity.alternative: Ego dissolution could leave impersonal or distributed experience without a numerically single universal subject.
charity.decisiveQualification: Persistence without ego does not establish universal identity across experiencers.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The model answers what the subject is, but the move from ego dissolution to numerical universal subjectivity leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Reports of residual experience support a distinction from ego, while universal identity and mode individuation remain substantially asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central subject-differentiation bridge by identifying individuals as modes of universal subjectivity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The answer supplies a serious deeper-subject model but does not adequately preserve the strongest non-universal interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes ego dissolution as falling back toward a universal core subjectivity while retaining experienced excitations and calls individuals patterns of that subjectivity.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: The green-elephant example still fails to locate causality because an ordinary non-lucid dream need contain no distinct self that causes its represented contents.
moves.attributionBasis: Blackmore explicitly says she remains puzzled, contrasts waking imagination with ordinary dreaming, and renews her causal challenge to Kastrup.

components.text: How the universal-subject account locates the immediate causal source in an ordinary dream without a distinct self.

response.rationale: The reply accepts that the elephant lacks autonomous causal power and presses the unresolved source of causation when no experienced personal agent is present.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts the remaining causal-bearer demand rather than merely disputing universal subjectivity in general.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is carefully limited to ordinary non-lucid dreams and clearly distinguishes represented content from an experienced agent.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker asks where causality resides and does not overstate the phenomenological premise as proving impossibility.

charity.alternative: A non-personal dreaming process could cause contents without appearing as a self within the dream.
charity.decisiveQualification: The ontology must still specify that process's causal identity and relation to universal subjectivity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The question consistently exposes that absence of a represented self does not identify the causal bearer invoked by the example.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The ordinary-dream phenomenology supports the challenge, although absence of a felt self does not show absence of all causal organization.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central causal-subject bridge by testing the proposed bearer in the example at issue.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge permits an unrepresented causal bearer but properly demands that the theory identify it.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt notes that an ordinary dream may lack a distinct self and asks where causal factors originate once the elephant itself is denied causal agency.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Causality arises from the intrinsic archetypal properties and natural self-excitation modes of the one universal field of subjectivity.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage directly answers Blackmore in Kastrup's analytic-idealist vocabulary and develops a sustained account of properties, excitation, and causality.

components.text: Where causal regularity comes from if neither the dream object nor an experienced personal self is fundamental.
What deeper entity bears the causal dispositions attributed to the personal “I.”

response.rationale: The reply locates causality in intrinsic properties and natural excitation modes of universal subjectivity rather than in dream characters or the narrative self.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers the location question directly, while the content and necessity of the posited intrinsic properties remain underexplained.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal-source thesis is recoverable, but archetypes, frequencies, harmonics, and excitation modes shift between metaphorical and explanatory uses.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Positing intrinsic dispositions is coherent, but calling them the root of all causality exceeds the warrant supplied in the span.

charity.alternative: A neutral process could possess the same intrinsic dispositions without being universal subjectivity.
charity.decisiveQualification: Dispositional structure does not independently establish the substrate's mental character.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Intrinsic properties can ground dispositions, but the inference risks circularity unless the properties and their production of regularity are independently specified.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Experiences in which time and space disintegrate raise doubts about their fundamentality and challenge explanations that implicitly presuppose spatiotemporal processes.
moves.attributionBasis: Blackmore identifies her long meditation experience, describes altered states in the first person, and explicitly asks Kastrup to address their implications.

components.text: Whether talk of fields, vibrations, frequencies, and processes covertly presupposes space and time.

response.rationale: The reply uses experiences of spatial and temporal disintegration to question fundamentality and to test whether the preceding causal imagery depends on spatiotemporal notions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the conceptual presupposition but mainly raises the challenge rather than fully defeating the causal account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The altered-state observation and the limited question about fundamentality are clearly distinguished from a conclusive ontological inference.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker treats the experiences as grounds for inquiry and doubt, not as proof that spacetime is nonfundamental.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Idealism can preserve nature's structure without spacetime by treating fundamental structure as semantic or cognitive relations whose meaning requires no extension.
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup is invited by name to make the final remark and delivers a continuous answer contrasting idealism with extension-dependent ontology.

components.text: How structured differentiation and meaningful relations can persist without fundamental spatial or temporal extension.

response.rationale: The reply directly proposes semantic and cognitive relations as real structure that carries meaning without requiring spatial or temporal extension.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers the decisive nonspatiotemporal-structure demand, although its example does not derive nature's full mathematical order.

precisionFindings.rationale: Cognitive relation, meaning, and extension are used consistently, with an implicit limit from illustrative relation to general natural structure.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims that nonextended meaningful relations are possible and uses friendship as an illustration, not as a complete cosmology.
